description: We are a cross-border collective of data enthusiasts, designers, and creative technologists based across Bangladesh, Cambodia, and Vietnam. Living in three delta nations profoundly shaped by monsoons and climate shifts, we share a deep, firsthand connection to the changing rhythms of our skies. By blending our diverse strengths in data engineering, interactive design, and hardware/software crafting, we turn raw meteorological data from cities around the world into living melodies.
summary: DeltaBeat is an interactive web experience that turns monthly NASA satellite imagery into music. Users can select Dhaka, Sylhet, Tonle Sap, or Huế and explore each place through a month-by-month sequence. As the imagery changes, the app translates rainfall patterns into musical notes. In its sound mapping, more notes represent wetter-than-normal conditions, while fewer represent drier-than-normal conditions. By pairing Earth imagery with dynamic sound, the project gives users another way to notice seasonal patterns that can be difficult to interpret from maps alone. It responds to NASA Space Apps’ Earth Information Jukebox challenge by making Earth science more engaging and multisensory, inviting people to listen to how conditions change across locations and months.
details:
DELTABEAT: EARTH’S MUSIC BOX

Hear the Earth. One record at a time.

Try it: Choose a place → Play its year → Flip the record → Hear what changed.

DeltaBeat is a working browser-based sonification experience by The Delta Force. It responds to The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing NASA Earth Information Center imagery with music synthesized during playback. A familiar record-player interface invites people to choose a place, hear its changing environment and inspect the evidence behind the sound.

Choose a place, a variable and a year, then play its record. DeltaBeat prototype interface, shown with its development title Earth Jukebox. Screenshot from the team’s current repository.

WHY WE BUILT IT

Earth imagery contains patterns that can be difficult to notice without experience reading maps and colour scales. Our starting point was a simple question: what would changing environmental conditions sound like in places connected to our communities? We began with Dhaka and Sylhet in Bangladesh, Tonle Sap in Cambodia and Huế in Vietnam. These places connect the science to city waterlogging, monsoon landscapes, a changing lake and a flood-affected coastal region. The current prototype also includes the Amazon near Manaus, Alice Springs and Tromsø, allowing comparisons across contrasting landscapes.

Our intended audience is secondary-school students and curious members of the public. We aim to support learning through several routes at once: listening, looking, reading and interacting. Sound is an additional way into the data; the images, explanations and tables remain available for people who prefer them.

WHAT A VISITOR CAN DO

The live version contains 30 discs: rain and greenness for seven places over two years, plus two exploratory snow-cover discs for Tromsø. Each disc represents one place, one variable and one year. Each musical bar represents a calendar month, so a year plays in about 24 seconds.

Choose a record by keyboard, click or drag, then press Play. The turntable animates, a monthly calendar follows the sound, and a nearby NASA map displays the place and date. Flip the record to compare the same calendar months in another year: rain uses 2025/2026 and greenness uses 2024/2025. Stop, pause or move between months to investigate a pattern. At the end of December the record returns to the shelf.

Science mode simplifies playback to one data note per month. The Details panel supplies a twelve-month table, chart, piano roll, reference image, source link, units, quality information and limitations. A guided tour introduces the controls. The current build includes 340 monthly map crops for months with available values.

Huế, November 2025: NASA imagery, the calendar and music follow the selected month. The chart compares the two selected years. Rain means wetter or drier than normal, not total rainfall. Source: NASA SVS 4897; interface by The Delta Force.

HOW NASA IMAGES BECOME SOUND

1. Our Python pipeline reads dated NASA Scientific Visualization Studio frames and samples a small geographic area around each agreed coordinate. It matches the image colours against the source colour key, aggregates sampled frames into monthly categories and writes a shared JSON file. Source-frame information, checks and evidence are retained in the repository.

2. Rain comes from NASA SVS 4897, based on GPM/IMERG precipitation visualizations. It represents wetter or drier conditions than normal, with a roughly three-month fading history. It is not a direct measurement of rainfall accumulated in that calendar month. Categories run from −4 to +4; displayed numeric values represent colour bands.

3. Greenness comes from NASA SVS 5544, the VIIRS vegetation visualization associated with the Earth Information Center. Because its displayed colour scale runs from low to high without numeric labels, we encode relative position on that scale and four greenness categories. We do not claim to recover exact physical NDVI values from the image.

4. JavaScript turns the monthly categories into an explicit note schedule. For rain, wetter categories sit higher and produce more data-note events; drier categories sit lower and produce fewer. For greenness, higher categories add musical layers. A fixed mapping is used across places and years so comparisons remain interpretable. Instrument-like timbres, harmony and quiet field recordings give each landscape a distinct atmosphere.

5. The Web Audio API synthesizes the scheduled music in real time. The NASA frame processing is performed beforehand; the browser does not claim to retrieve live satellite measurements. The map shown for a month is a representative dated frame, while the rain and greenness categories can combine several sampled frames from that month.

An example makes the mapping concrete: a sampled rain colour in the “2–5 mm/day drier than normal” band becomes level −1. The music uses the corresponding lower, less-dense pattern, while the text explains the same category. A transparent near-normal rain pixel is treated according to that rain visualization's meaning; an unavailable month is separately marked missing.

WHAT MAKES THE EXPERIENCE DISTINCTIVE

The record metaphor carries scientific meaning. Side A/B makes year-to-year comparison tangible. A scratched record signals missing months, and a break in source continuity can produce a skip. Missing months have no data melody; Music mode uses crackle as a cue rather than inventing a value. These conditions also appear in text and visual markings.

The collection connects local stories to global imagery. People can begin with a familiar place and explore another landscape using the same interpretation rules. The musical arrangement invites sustained attention, while Science mode and the evidence panel make the underlying choices inspectable. Our instrumental styles are creative interpretations, not claims to reproduce a culture's traditional music authentically.

ACCESSIBILITY AND INTENDED IMPACT

Controls are real HTML buttons with keyboard support, focus handling and screen-reader announcements. The interface offers high contrast, reduced motion, volume adjustment and optional focus preview. Month tables and visual categories provide a route to the information without relying on hearing or colour alone. Keyboard shortcuts cover playback, month navigation, flipping, mode switching and details.

We hope to help learners notice patterns, ask better questions and connect Earth observations to places they care about. Potential settings include classroom activities, science clubs and informal public demonstrations. Learning gains and accessibility outcomes have not yet been established through a formal user study. Broader testing with screen-reader users, people with different hearing and visual needs, and mobile devices is a priority.

VALIDATION AND SCIENTIFIC LIMITS

The project includes automated checks for the data format, missing-month flags, note scheduling, comparisons and keyboard behaviour. A round-trip check reconstructs the encoded monthly categories from the note schedule; the repository reports agreement across all 360 month slots in the current 30-disc dataset. This validates the encoding, not the accuracy of the underlying environmental observations.

Rain colour bands lose detail and saturate at their extremes. Relative greenness is not a measured NDVI value. Small image patches represent surrounding areas rather than individual streets or households. Two selected years cannot establish a long-term climate trend, and the project is an educational prototype rather than a flood forecast or emergency-warning system. Historical events in the place introductions provide context and are not automatically events represented by the selected disc years.

The additional MODIS Terra snow layer uses monthly GIBS imagery and remains exploratory. Transparent pixels can represent zero snow or unavailable observations, so its colour-derived area estimates require further validation with original product quality and land masks. Rain and greenness are the primary demonstration of our documented image-to-category method. Unpublished months remain missing.

TOOLS, TEAMWORK AND SI DISCLOSURE

The implementation uses Python with Pillow, NumPy and requests for image processing; HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Canvas for the interface; the browser Web Audio API for synthesis; pytest and Node.js tests for validation; FFmpeg for preparing field recordings and demonstration clips; and GitHub/GitHub Pages for collaboration and public hosting. The deployed app requires no account or special hardware beyond a compatible browser and audio output.

The team originated the jukebox concept and directed the stories, appearance, scope, listening decisions and review. Claude/Claude Code and OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, debugging, data processing, tests, research, design exploration and documentation. ChatGPT also helped explain technical concepts and draft content; this submission text was prepared with Codex assistance. We selected SI categories to disclose those contributions, including design refinement, rather than implying that an SI model invented the team's core concept. The product's music is generated by deterministic code, not by a hosted generative-music model.

The repository documents pre-event research, notes, a reference mockup and a generic accessible page template; the product implementation, data processing and sound work were developed during November 14–15. An AI-generated mockup served as a planning reference. In the product, the console and disc art are drawn by code, story-card artwork is adapted from credited photographs, and background sounds are real licensed field recordings. Full credits, adaptation details and SI use are linked below. Third-party assets retain their own licences.

NEXT STEPS

We would prioritize user testing, stronger source-quality handling, additional reviewed place descriptions and accessible explanations before expanding the collection. The common data format and explicit sound mapping make it possible to add further verified NASA visualizations without changing how visitors learn to interpret the experience.
